assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Litmus
items.clue: Red in one kind of solution and blue in the opposite kind.

items.label: Reaction arrow
items.clue: The sign in an equation that means 'change into' or 'make'

items.label: Universal indicator
items.clue: Shows a range of colours, from red through green to purple.

questions.stem: Which statement is true of every acid?

options.text: It eats away any material it touches
It can be neutralised by an alkali
It has the same pH as all other acids
It bubbles and fizzes on its own

questions.explanation: Yes. Every acid reacts with an alkali and is neutralised, making a salt and water. That is how acids and alkalis are defined.

questions.stem: A substance dissolves in water. Which result shows that the substance is an alkali?

options.text: It neutralises acids
It turns blue litmus red
It has a pH below 7
It reacts with nothing

questions.explanation: Yes. A substance that dissolves in water and neutralises acids is a base that dissolves: an alkali. Its solution also has a pH above 7.

questions.stem: When an alkali neutralises an acid, what happens to the acid?

options.text: It breaks down on its own and stops being acid
It reacts with the alkali to make a salt
It is simply stopped from burning anything
It is only diluted by the water in the alkali

questions.explanation: Yes. Neutralisation is a reaction between the acid and the alkali. It makes a salt and water.

questions.stem: What happens in a neutralisation reaction?

options.text: An acid and an alkali react and cancel out
An acid is diluted with water until it is safe
An acid and an alkali just mix together
An alkali destroys an acid and is unchanged

questions.explanation: In neutralisation an acid reacts with an alkali (or another base), and each cancels out the other.

questions.stem: Some indigestion tablets contain magnesium hydroxide, a base. How do they ease pain caused by too much stomach acid?

options.text: They soak up the acid without reacting
They react with the acid and neutralise it
They cool the acid so that it stops burning
They add acid to help digest the food

questions.explanation: The base in the tablet reacts with some of the excess acid and neutralises it.

questions.stem: A farmer's soil is too acidic for the crop. What should be added to the soil?

options.text: A neutral substance such as salt, to neutralise it
A weak acid such as vinegar, to weaken the acid
A lot of water, to wash the acid out for good
A base such as lime, to neutralise the acid

questions.explanation: Lime is a base, so it reacts with the acid in the soil and neutralises it.

options.text: A soft metal that reacts with water
A soluble base that neutralises acids
A neutral liquid with a pH of 7
A harmless liquid that waters acids down

questions.explanation: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water; it neutralises acids.

questions.stem: Alkali is added to an acid a little at a time, until far more has been added than is needed to neutralise it. What is the mixture now?

options.text: Neutral, as the acid has been cancelled out
Acidic, as it started off as an acid
Alkaline, as there is alkali left over
Both strongly acidic and strongly alkaline

questions.explanation: Once all the acid has reacted, any extra alkali stays in the mixture and makes it alkaline.

questions.stem: Which pair of substances would react together in a neutralisation reaction?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide
Hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid
Sodium hydroxide and distilled water
Hydrochloric acid and magnesium metal

questions.explanation: Neutralisation needs an acid and a base: hydrochloric acid is an acid, sodium hydroxide an alkali.
